content: The Guidelines for the Prevention, Care, and Treatment of Persons with Chronic Hepatitis B Infection, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in March 2015, provide comprehensive recommendations for managing chronic hepatitis B (CHB). These guidelines address prevention, diagnosis, and treatment strategies, with a focus on lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) where the burden of hepatitis B is highest. Chronic hepatitis B is defined as the persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for six months or more after acute infection. It is a significant global health issue, affecting an estimated 240 million people worldwide, with complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) leading to approximately 650,000 deaths annually. The guidelines emphasize the importance of universal hepatitis B immunization programs targeting infants, particularly with a birth dose, which have proven effective in reducing the incidence and prevalence of hepatitis B in endemic regions. However, these programs will not immediately impact HBV-related deaths, as the benefits will be realized over decades. Antiviral therapies, such as tenofovir and entecavir, are available and have been shown to suppress HBV replication, prevent progression to cirrhosis, and reduce the risk of HCC and liver-related mortality. Despite their effectiveness, these treatments do not eradicate the virus in most cases, necessitating lifelong therapy. Access to these drugs remains limited in LMICs, delaying timely intervention to prevent advanced liver disease. The WHO guidelines are structured along the continuum of care for CHB, from initial assessment of disease stage and treatment eligibility to initiation of first-line antiviral therapy, monitoring for disease progression and drug toxicity, and switching to second-line drugs in cases of treatment failure. They recommend the use of simple, non-invasive diagnostic tests to assess liver disease and prioritize treatment for individuals with advanced liver disease or those at the highest risk of mortality. The preferred firstand second-line treatments are nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high barrier to drug resistance, such as tenofovir and entecavir. Lifelong treatment is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis, along with regular monitoring for disease progression, drug toxicity, and early detection of HCC. Special considerations are provided for specific populations, including individuals co-infected with HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), or hepatitis D virus (HDV), as well as children, adolescents, and pregnant women. Recommendations for HBV/HIV co-infected individuals align with the WHO 2013 Consolidated Guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs, which are being updated. The use of interferon or pegylated interferon is excluded from these guidelines due to their high cost, significant adverse effects, and limited feasibility in LMICs. The guidelines also summarize existing WHO recommendations for preventing HBV transmission, including perinatal and early childhood vaccination, catch-up vaccination for key populations, and strategies to prevent transmission in healthcare settings. Additionally, they highlight the role of alcohol reduction interventions in slowing liver disease progression in individuals with CHB. Future updates to these guidelines will address topics such as hepatitis B and C testing algorithms, acute hepatitis B and C management, and advanced liver disease care. Updated recommendations on hepatitis B vaccination will be issued by the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE). These guidelines aim to support country program managers and healthcare providers in planning and scaling up hepatitis B prevention, care, and treatment efforts, particularly in resource-limited settings.
